description.sr_latin: Kratke, ponovljive rečenice koje pokazuju kako se sklapaju misli — hoću, mogu, moram, idem, daj mi.
description.en: Short, reusable sentence frames that show how thoughts get assembled — want, can, must, go, give me. Swap the fillers and say almost anything.

phrases.context: Tell your girlfriend you're worn out and ready to crash for the night.
phrases.notes: The core frame: 'hoću da' + present verb = 'I want to ___'. Serbian has no infinitive here — literally 'I want that I sleep'.

phrases.en: I don't want to get up.
phrases.context: It's a lazy weekend morning and you groan to your girlfriend, still under the covers.
phrases.notes: 'Neću' is the negated 'hoću' — one word, not 'ne hoću'. Same 'da' + verb frame.

phrases.context: Suggest to your girlfriend that the two of you grab something to eat now.
phrases.notes: 'Hoćeš da ...?' is the everyday way to suggest doing something together — softer than a command.

phrases.context: Your friend is wrestling with something and you step in to offer a hand.
phrases.notes: 'Pomoći' takes the dative, so 'ti' (to you). Clitic order: 'da ti pomognem'.

phrases.context: Turn to your friend because you can't manage a task on your own.
phrases.notes: 'Možeš li da ...?' = 'can you ...?'; 'li' marks the question. 'Mi' (to me) is dative because 'pomoći' takes it.

phrases.context: Tell your girlfriend you can't come out because the job needs you right now.
phrases.notes: 'Moram da' + verb = 'I have to ___'. Stronger obligation than 'treba da' (should).

phrases.context: Push your friend to have something after he's skipped meals all day.
phrases.notes: Same 'moraš da' + verb obligation, aimed at someone else: 'you have to ___'. 'Jedeš' is the 'you' form of 'jesti'.

phrases.context: It's getting late and you let your friend know you ought to head off soon.
phrases.notes: 'Treba da' + verb = 'I should / ought to ___'. 'Treba' stays in the 3rd person — it doesn't change for the subject.

phrases.context: Admit to your friend, flatly, that you can't pull this off without a hand.
phrases.notes: Different frame: 'treba mi X' = 'I need X' (literally 'X is needed to me'). The thing you need is the subject; you are the dative 'mi'.

phrases.context: You're parched and tell your girlfriend what would sort you out right now.
phrases.notes: Same 'treba mi X' frame: the thing needed ('voda') is nominative subject; you are the dative 'mi'.

phrases.context: Your girlfriend keeps offering snacks and drinks, and you turn it all down.
phrases.notes: Here 'hteti' takes a direct object, not 'da'. The double negative is normal: 'neću ništa' = lit. 'I-won't nothing'.

phrases.context: The bottle is right by your girlfriend, so you ask her to pour you a little.
phrases.notes: 'Daj mi' + thing = 'give me ___'. Genitive 'vode' means 'some water', a partial amount — very natural for food and drink.

phrases.context: You point at an object near your friend and ask him to hand it straight over.
phrases.notes: Same 'daj mi' frame with a full object: 'to' (that) is accusative, the whole thing rather than a partial amount.

phrases.context: The bread basket is down the other end, so you ask your girlfriend to send it your way.
phrases.notes: 'Dodaj' (from 'dodati') is specifically 'pass / hand over', perfect at the table. Serbian 'hleb', Bosnian 'hljeb'.

phrases.context: Your girlfriend is heading to the kitchen anyway, so you call after her for a glass.
phrases.notes: 'Donesi' = bring (it here), unlike 'dodaj' (pass) or 'daj' (give). Genitive 'vode' again signals 'some water'.

phrases.context: The coffees you ordered are waiting at the counter; ask your friend to carry them over.
phrases.notes: Accusative 'kafu' here = the specific coffee (the whole cup), versus genitive 'kafe' for 'some coffee'.

phrases.context: Before launching into a favour, you check whether your friend is free right now.
phrases.notes: 'Imaš li ...?' = 'do you have ...?'. After this kind of question the noun often goes genitive: 'vremena'.

phrases.context: You've just arrived at your friend's place and ask whether there's any coffee going.
phrases.notes: Genitive 'kafe' = 'any/some coffee' (an unspecified amount), the natural case after 'imaš li' for a substance.

phrases.context: You can't find the bottle anywhere and ask your girlfriend where it ended up.
phrases.notes: 'Gde je ___?' = 'where is ___?'. Swap in any noun.

phrases.en: Shall we go for a beer?
phrases.context: Work's done and you nudge your friend to head out for a drink together.
phrases.notes: 'Idemo na ___?' = 'shall we go for ___?'. Use 'na' + accusative for activities: 'na pivo', 'na kafu', 'na ručak'.

phrases.context: You'd rather ask than order, so you check if your girlfriend can grab you some water.
phrases.notes: Politer than the bare imperative 'donesi'. Combines 'možeš li da' with the bring-frame.

phrases.context: Grabbing your keys, you tell your girlfriend you're popping into the centre for a bit.
phrases.notes: 'Idem u' + place (accusative) = 'I'm going to ___'. Motion toward a place uses 'u' + accusative: 'u grad'.

phrases.context: The night's winding down and you tell your friend you're calling it and heading home.
phrases.notes: 'Kući' is a fixed form meaning 'home(ward)' — no preposition needed.

phrases.context: You're hungry and let your girlfriend know you're off to the kitchen to get food.
phrases.notes: 'Idem da' + verb = 'I'm going (in order) to ___'. Expresses purpose.

phrases.context: You let your friend know you're stepping out to the café down the street for a bit.
phrases.notes: For activities and events Serbian uses 'na' + accusative: 'na kafu', 'na pivo', 'na ručak'.

phrases.context: Dinner's on the table and you call your girlfriend over so you can both dig in.
phrases.notes: 'Hajde da' + we-form = 'let's ___'. The verb takes the 'we' ending ('jedemo').

phrases.context: You've both lingered long enough and you nudge your friend that it's time to head out.
phrases.notes: Same 'hajde da' + we-form, here with 'idemo' (we go): the everyday 'let's go / come on'.

phrases.context: It's getting late and you text your girlfriend to find out if she's on her way back.
phrases.notes: Imperfective 'dolaziš' fits a general 'are you coming (tonight)?' question.

phrases.en: I'll be there in five minutes.
phrases.context: Your friend is already waiting, so you text that you're nearly at the meeting spot.
phrases.notes: 'Za' + time = 'in / within (that much time)'. After 'pet' (5+) the noun goes genitive plural: 'minuta'.

phrases.context: You're only stepping out for a second and reassure your girlfriend you won't be long.
phrases.notes: Reflexive 'se' stays attached to 'vraćam' (I return). 'Odmah' = right away / immediately.

phrases.context: You're wrapping up a chat with your friend and sign off until you meet again.
phrases.notes: 'Vidimo se' = 'we'll see each other' (reflexive). Swap the ending: 'sutra' (tomorrow), 'večeras' (tonight).

phrases.context: You got to the restaurant first and text your girlfriend that you're sitting there for her.
phrases.notes: 'Čekati' takes a direct object (accusative), so 'te' (you) — no preposition, unlike English 'wait FOR'.

phrases.en: What do you want to do?
phrases.context: The evening's wide open and you ask your girlfriend how she'd like to spend it together.
phrases.notes: 'Šta hoćeš da ...?' = 'what do you want (us/me) to ...?'. The verb after 'da' takes a personal ending — here 'radimo' (we).

phrases.context: Your girlfriend has gone quiet and seems off, so you gently check in on how she is.
phrases.notes: 'Jesi li ...?' is the stressed question form of the clitic 'si'. 'Dobro' = okay/well (adverb).

phrases.en: Do you want to come with me?
phrases.context: You're about to head out the door and turn to invite your girlfriend to come along.
phrases.notes: 'Hoćeš li ...?' = 'do you want ...?'. 'Sa mnom' = 'with me' — 'sa' takes the instrumental, here 'mnom' from 'ja'.

phrases.context: You're both turning in for the night and you wish your girlfriend a warm goodnight.
phrases.notes: 'Lepo' here is the adverb 'nicely / well'. A warm bedtime line.

phrases.context: Your friend teases you for sleeping in, and you happily own up to loving your bed.
phrases.notes: 'Volim da' + verb = 'I love (doing) ___'. A habit or general liking.

phrases.en: I love it when you're here.
phrases.context: A quiet evening together at home, and you tell your girlfriend how much you like her around.
phrases.notes: 'Volim kad ...' = 'I love it when ...'. 'Kad' (when) introduces the situation; 'tu' = here/around.

phrases.en: I hate it when you're late.
phrases.context: Your friend rolls in late yet again, and you give him grief about always keeping you waiting.
phrases.notes: Mirror of 'volim kad'. 'Kasniš' = 'you're (running) late' (from 'kasniti').

phrases.context: It's around lunchtime and you check whether your friend is up for grabbing some food.
phrases.notes: 'Gladan' is the masculine form; say 'gladna' to a woman. The adjective agrees with the listener's gender.

phrases.context: You've locked in plans for this evening and sign off with your girlfriend until then.
phrases.notes: Same 'vidimo se' frame fixed to a time: 'večeras' = tonight/this evening.

phrases.context: Your friend proposes a plan and you give an easy, agreeable yes to it.
phrases.notes: Literally 'it's possible', but used constantly as 'okay / works for me / sure'.

phrases.context: Ask your girlfriend to wait a second while you finish something.
phrases.notes: 'Samo malo' literally 'only a little' — the everyday 'hang on a sec / one moment'.

phrases.context: Your girlfriend frets over a small slip-up and you wave it off to put her at ease.
phrases.notes: 'Nije' is the negative of 'je' (is). Lit. 'it's not terrible' — a warm 'no big deal / don't worry about it'.

phrases.en: Get in touch. / Let me know.
phrases.context: You're saying bye to your friend and ask him to drop you a line once he's free.
phrases.notes: 'Javiti se' = to get in touch / drop a line; the 'se' belongs to the verb. 'Mi' (to me) is the dative.

phrases.context: Your girlfriend shares some good news and you react with genuine, warm approval.
phrases.notes: 'Baš' intensifies — 'really / so'. 'Baš lepo' = 'that's really nice'.

phrases.context: Your friend is getting worked up and rushing, so you tell him to ease off and relax.
phrases.notes: 'Polako' means 'slowly / easy / no rush' — quintessentially Serbian, both a reply and a whole philosophy.

phrases.context: Your girlfriend asks a small favour she already knows you'll do, and you say yes warmly.
phrases.notes: 'Naravno' = of course / naturally. A warm, emphatic yes that needs no extra words.

phrases.context: Your friend apologizes for showing up late and you brush it off so he stops fussing.
phrases.notes: 'Nema' = 'there isn't'. The thing that isn't there goes genitive: 'problema'.

phrases.context: Your friend asks you something you genuinely don't know, so you shrug it off.
phrases.notes: Very common shrug. 'Pojma' (of a clue/idea) is genitive after the negative 'nemam'.
